title: High-dimensional Analysis of Synthetic Data Selection
claim: Covariance mismatch between synthetic and target data drives excess risk, while mean alignment has no effect, matching theory.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row, shared legend style, theory lines with empirical dots
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the y-axis label 'Excess risk' and the same legend. The legend gives three colored curves for rho_s = 0.9 (dark purple), 0.5 (blue) and 0.1 (teal). Solid lines show theory, and dots with shaded bands show empirical results. Panel (a) plots risk against the cosine similarity of the means. The three curves are flat horizontal lines, with teal highest at about 0.75, blue at about 0.45 and purple at about 0.33. This shows the mean has no effect. Panel (b) plots risk against n_s/p. The curves decay from about 0.35 to about 0.1, and larger rho_s gives lower risk. Panel (c) plots risk against covariance scale. The curves also decay, and the ordering by rho_s is the same. Theory and empirical points agree closely. The eye goes first to the flat lines in (a).
caption: Excess risk using training data from N(µt, Σt) and synthetic data from N(µs, Σs), where Σt, Σs are Kac–Murdock–Szegö matrices (Toeplitz matrices with geometrically decaying entries) with parameters ρt, ρs, scaled so that Tr[M ⊤M] = p. We pick ∥µt∥2 = ∥µs∥2 = 2√p, ρt = 0.9, p = 600, nt = 1200, ns = 1200, unless varying the parameters in the plot. Each value is computed from 100 i.i.d. trials, the error band is at 1 standard deviation, and theoretical predictions are continuous lines. Different curves correspond to different values of ρs. (a) Changing the cosine similarity of the mean does not impact the risk (here, Σs is scaled by η := ρs). (b) Larger ρs gives lower risk since Σs is closer to Σt. (c) Scaling Σs reduces the risk.
abstract: Despite the progress in the development of generative models, their usefulness in creating synthetic data that improve prediction performance of classifiers has been put into question. Besides heuristic principles such as "synthetic data should be close to the real data distribution", it is actually not clear which specific properties affect the generalization error. Our paper addresses this question through the lens of high-dimensional regression. Theoretically, we show that, for linear models, the covariance shift between the target distribution and the distribution of the synthetic data affects the generalization error but, surprisingly, the mean shift does not. Furthermore we prove that, in some settings, matching the covariance of the target distribution is optimal. Remarkably, the theoretical insights from linear models carry over to deep neural networks and generative models. We empirically demonstrate that the covariance matching procedure (matching the covariance of the synthetic data with that of the data coming from the target distribution) performs well against several recent approaches for synthetic data selection, across training paradigms, architectures, datasets and generative models used for augmentation.
